# The Saltmere Harbor Almanac

Saltmere is a small fishing town on a cold northern bay. This almanac describes its fish market, its boats, its lighthouse, its sailing school and its yearly Lantern Night festival.

## The Fish Market

Herring is the heart of Saltmere. Every morning the herring boats come in before dawn, and herring is sold smoked, pickled, salted and fresh. Visitors say the whole town smells of herring. Mackerel and cod are the next most popular fish, and most families eat cod on Fridays.

Further back in the market, smaller stalls sell pollock, hake, turbot, ling, gurnard, megrim and garfish. One stall run by the Dunlin family sells only John Dory, which locals call "the thumbprint fish" because of the dark spot on its side. In late autumn a single stall sells pouting, a small fish most visitors have never heard of.[^1]

## Boats in the Harbor

The most famous boat in Saltmere is The Gannet, a blue herring drifter that has fished the bay for sixty years. Almost every postcard of the town shows The Gannet at the harbor wall.

Other working boats include the Morning Pell, the Brackwater and the Hollow Bell. The smallest boat in the harbor is the Little Rennet, a rowing boat used to ferry crates between larger boats. An old crabber called Tamsin's Luck is moored at the far end of the harbor and goes out only in summer.[^2]

## The Lighthouse

Saltmere Light stands on the rocks at the mouth of the bay. Its first keeper was Hester Vane, who kept the light burning for thirty-one winters. After her came Isaac Morrow and then Edith Larch. The light was made automatic in 1974, and its last keeper, Tobias Quill, now runs the small lighthouse museum.

## The Sailing School

Children in Saltmere learn to sail at the harbor school. Every child must first learn the bowline, which the teachers call "the only knot that matters". After that come the figure-eight knot and the cleat hitch. Older students learn the sheet bend and the rolling hitch. The best students are taught the Turk's head, a decorative knot woven around the tiller.[^3]

## Lantern Night

Lantern Night is held on the last Saturday of October. Paper lanterns are floated across the harbor, and the whole town eats outdoors along the harbor wall.

Fish pie is the most famous Lantern Night food, and nearly every family brings one. Crab cakes and saffron buns are almost as common. Smaller stalls sell smoked eel on toast, nettle soup, samphire fritters and sea-buckthorn jelly. The rarest treat is burnt-honey fudge, made by only one baker in town.[^4]

## Footnotes

[^1]: The market has never sold salmon. A town rule from 1911 keeps all salmon for the river traps upstream, so a visitor asking for salmon will be sent away.

[^2]: Tamsin's Luck is named after Tamsin Dunlin, who caught a record turbot from it in 1952.

[^3]: Older sailors also remember the Saltmere slip, a quick-release knot invented in the town, but it is no longer taught.

[^4]: Before 1990, Lantern Night also had stalls selling whelks in vinegar, but they were stopped after a bad harvest.
